```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96)
```

## What it does

`hkselect` chooses housekeeper (reference) genes for normalizing quantitative RT-PCR data. Within
one tissue type, it fits a two-way model of log expression with its own error variance for each
gene (Model 1a) and ranks single genes and gene sets by the standard deviation of their log
geometric mean. Across tissue types, it fits a model whose error standard deviation is a gene
factor times a tissue factor, with a tissue-specific bias for each gene (Model 2), and finds the
gene set of each size whose largest mean squared error over tissue types is smallest.

Szabo A, Perou CM, Karaca M, Perreard L, Palais R, Quackenbush JF, Bernard PS. Statistical
modeling for selecting housekeeper genes. *Genome Biology* 5:R59 (2004).
doi:10.1186/gb-2004-5-8-r59. The authors never released their code; this package was rebuilt
from the paper's text in the [fossil](https://github.com/jeonglab-bcm/fossil) repository.

## Install

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jeonglab-bcm/fossil/PMC507884/package")
```

```{r load}
library(hkselect)
packageVersion("hkselect")
```

## Example input

The paper's breast cancer data: relative copy numbers of six candidate housekeepers in 80
primary breast tumours (Additional data file 1 of the paper).

```{r input}
breast <- read_expression(example_path("szabo2004_breast.csv"))
dim(breast$expr)
head(breast$expr, 3)
```

## Run the method: one tissue type

Model 1a, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood, gives each gene's error standard deviation on
the natural-log scale, with a 95% interval.

```{r model1}
ci <- gene_sd_ci(breast$expr)
ci[order(ci$sd), ]
```

The standard deviation of the log geometric mean of the best set of each size:

```{r sets}
sets <- best_sets(gene_sd(fit_model1(breast$expr)))
sets
```

```{r plot-sets, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(sets$size, sets$sd, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "Genes in the set",
     ylab = "SD of the log geometric mean", ylim = c(0, max(sets$sd)))
```

The paper picks the three-gene set MRPL19, PSMC4 and PUM1: the four-gene set is barely better.

## Compare with the expected output

The expected output is the paper's Tables 1 and 2 as printed. Gene sets are compared as sets;
Table 1 at its printed precision (0.0005) and Table 2 within one unit in its last digit (0.0001),
because its six-gene value comes out 0.1514 against 0.1513 printed.

```{r compare}
expected <- read.csv(example_path("szabo2004_expected.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
t1 <- expected[expected$table == "table1", ]
t2 <- expected[expected$table == "table2", ]
sd <- gene_sd(fit_model1(breast$expr))
same_set <- function(a, b) setequal(strsplit(a, "[,;]")[[1]], strsplit(b, "[,;]")[[1]])
ok1 <- abs(sd[t1$key] - t1$value) <= 0.0005 + 1e-12
ok2 <- unname(mapply(same_set, sets$genes, t2$genes))
ok3 <- abs(sets$sd - t2$value) <= 0.0001 + 1e-12
data.frame(size = sets$size, ours = round(sets$sd, 4), paper = t2$value, set_matches = ok2)
cat(sum(ok1), "of", length(ok1), "Table 1 values,", sum(ok2), "of", length(ok2), "Table 2 sets and",
    sum(ok3), "of", length(ok3), "Table 2 values match the expected output\n")
stopifnot(all(ok1), all(ok2), all(ok3))
```

geNorm, for comparison: its stepwise M-values give the same order as Model 1a except that PUM1
and PSMC4 swap, and leave MRPL19 and PSMC4 as an unordered best pair.

```{r genorm}
genorm(breast$expr)
```

## Run the method: several tissue types

The bundled multi-tissue data are synthetic: five genes in three tissue types of 60 samples,
drawn from Model 2 with known parameters (the paper's multi-tissue data, from Vandesompele et
al. 2002, carry no redistribution licence).

```{r model2}
synth <- read_expression(example_path("synthetic_tissues.csv"))
table(synth$tissue)
comp <- model2_components(fit_model2(synth$expr, synth$tissue))
round(comp$sigma, 3)
round(comp$varsigma, 3)
round(comp$bias, 3)
```

Each gene's mean squared error in each tissue type is its squared bias plus its variance
(the paper's Figure 3), signed here by the bias:

```{r mse-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
m <- gene_mse(comp)
barplot(matrix(m$signed_mse, nrow = 3, dimnames = list(unique(m$tissue), unique(m$gene))),
        beside = TRUE, legend.text = TRUE, ylab = "Signed MSE", args.legend = list(x = "topright"))
```

The best set of at most each size by the minimax criterion (Table 4 of the paper):

```{r minimax}
minimax_sets(comp)
```

The estimates against the parameters the data were drawn from (the expected output), allowing
15% for the standard deviations and 0.25 for the biases (about three standard errors):

```{r compare2}
truth <- read.csv(example_path("synthetic_truth.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s <- truth[truth$parameter == "sigma", ]; v <- truth[truth$parameter == "varsigma", ]
b <- truth[truth$parameter == "bias", ]
kg <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(b$key, ":"))
ok <- c(abs(comp$sigma[s$key] / s$value - 1) <= 0.15, abs(comp$varsigma[v$key] / v$value - 1) <= 0.15,
        abs(comp$bias[kg] - b$value) <= 0.25)
cat(sum(ok), "of", length(ok), "parameters match the values the data were drawn from\n")
stopifnot(all(ok))
```

## Your own data

- **Input:** a CSV with one row per sample: a `sample` column, a `tissue` column for Model 2,
  and one column per gene with positive expression levels on their original scale (relative copy
  numbers or 2^-Cq; not logs). Read it with `read_expression()`, or pass a numeric matrix with
  samples in rows and genes in columns.
- **One tissue type:** `gene_sd_ci(expr)` ranks the genes (`sd` is the error standard deviation
  of the log expression); `best_sets(gene_sd(fit_model1(expr)))` gives the best set of each size
  and the standard deviation of its log geometric mean, roughly the coefficient of variation of
  the normalizer on the original scale.
- **Several tissue types:** `comp <- model2_components(fit_model2(expr, tissue))`, then
  `gene_mse(comp)` (bias, variance and MSE of each gene in each tissue type) and
  `minimax_sets(comp)`. `set_mse(comp, set, bias = "mean")` uses the mean of the biases of the
  set; the default, `"sum"`, is the rule that reproduces the paper's Table 4.
- Compare models with `BIC()`: `fit_model1(expr, "common")` and `fit_model1(expr, "exchangeable")`
  are the paper's Models 1b and 1c; `fit_model2()` takes the competitors it compared Model 2 with.

## The reproduction

The full reproduction of the paper (Figures 1-3, Tables 1-4 and the claims in the text, on the
paper's data and Vandesompele et al.'s) is in `PMC507884/` of the
[fossil repository](https://github.com/jeonglab-bcm/fossil/tree/main/PMC507884), with its results
page at <https://jeonglab-bcm.github.io/fossil/PMC507884/>.
